title: Anti-immigration group’s tour of the Maritimes draws criticism
summary: The Dominion Society made stops in Charlottetown, Fredericton and Halifax trying to attract new members. Some local residents say there’s no room in the Maritimes for the group’s message of division.

image.caption: Daniel Tyrie founded the Dominion Society in 2025. (Brian MacKay/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
The Dominion Society made stops in Charlottetown, Fredericton and Halifax trying to attract new members. Some local residents say there’s no room in the Maritimes for the group’s message of division.
The group, which advocates for a policy it calls 'remigration,' says it has 4,000 members across Canada
An anti-immigration group’s recent tour of the Maritime provinces has drawn criticism from some residents who say there’s no room for the group’s message of division.
The Dominion Society of Canada made stops earlier this month in Charlottetown, Fredericton and Halifax trying to attract new members.
The organization, founded last year, focuses on “Canadian nationalism and Canadian heritage,” according to founder Daniel Tyrie.
“We promote an idea called remigration,” Tyrie said in an interview in Halifax after the tour.
“Which is a bundle of policies aimed to not only reduce mass immigration, but to reverse the flows of it and send people back through public policy.”

blocks.text: Tyrie said the belief that motivates its members is that most immigrants who have come to Canada in recent years “don't have any interest in integrating into our society.”
Tyrie said the Dominion Society uses social media with the aim of influencing Canadian culture and, in turn, changing Canadian immigration policy.
But Fredericton resident Jeff Britton said the group has it all wrong. He said many of his neighbours are immigrants from places like Nepal, India and Syria.
“They're great people,” said Britton.
“There's a social contract with immigrants to be kind and welcoming and those kinds of things. And, yeah, it's been really great to meet them.”
Joanna Dinan, who also lives in Fredericton, said she saw Dominion Society posters on Halloween and removed them once she realized their message.
“It was calling for remigration, which is essentially mass deportation of immigrants. And so I took it down because I thought it was rather egregious,” said Dinan.
She said she sees no evidence that multiculturalism isn’t working.
“My community is thriving and my community is a multicultural one. So I just don't think that there is any substance to their claim.”
Britton also tore down the group's promotional material, saying neither the Dominion Society nor its posters are welcome in his neighbourhood.

blocks.text: David Mitchell, the mayor of Bridgewater, N.S., had a similar message after learning the group had shared a photo on Facebook of posters in the town.
“Our community is changing, yes. That is not a bad thing,” said Mitchell.
“These are doctors, lawyers, engineers, people coming to build a life here. They're contributing to the economy. They're bringing their culture, but again, that's not a bad thing.”
Tyrie said that while the group's tour of the Maritimes focused on capital cities, it might consider visits to more rural communities in the future.
He said the group has 4,000 members countrywide, including more than 100 in Nova Scotia. He said around 50 people showed for its event at The Lower Deck in downtown Halifax on Nov. 14.
The bar said in a written statement that the organization’s affiliation was not disclosed when it booked the venue.

“We believe the booking was intentionally deceptive and did not accurately represent the identity of the group. Had we been aware of the nature of the organization, we would not have accepted the booking,” read the statement.
Group’s anti-immigration views touted on Maritime tour

In response to the group’s growing online presence and membership numbers, the Canadian Anti-Hate Network released a report in August identifying the group as a white nationalist organization, rather than simply a nationalist organization as it describes itself.
The network’s executive director, Evan Balgord, said talking about Canada’s immigration policies is fair game.

“But when they're talking about how particular groups are responsible for problems in society or fundamentally incompatible, you are straying into something that is racist and something that is hate speech,” he said.
The report also alleges that several members of the group have publicly identified as neo-Nazis.
Tyrie says he pays no mind to such critiques and isn’t concerned with the ideology that motivates his group’s members.
“If you agree with our main principle, our guiding principle, you're invited,” he said.

Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser, the MP for Central Nova, said that while he’s aware of the group’s activities across the country, he’s not “personally engaged in any sort of way with the organization.”
“When we tend to engage more directly, it’s typically when we see that there have been crimes committed, where there’s a public safety threat that needs to be managed,” he said.
The RCMP has not responded to an inquiry about whether there are any ongoing investigations into members of the Dominion Society related to criminal hate speech.
